title: RCSC SALAMI CTF Writeup
content:
Eid is a time of joy, surprises, and gifts — but this time, the celebration came wrapped in challenges instead of salami. The Eid Salami CTF blended festive storytelling with classic Capture The Flag techniques, turning simple Eid wishes into puzzles that tested observation, patience, and creative problem-solving skills.



This CTF featured a mix of file forensics, OSINT, terminal tricks, and logical exploitation, each problem cleverly disguised as an Eid tradition. From a “picture” that wasn’t really a picture, to a currency note hiding historical metadata, from invisible flags inside heartfelt stories to a deceptive Netcat service that rewarded patience over brute force — every challenge carried a unique lesson.

What made this CTF especially enjoyable was how real-world concepts were woven into playful narratives:

A corrupted PNG that turned out to be a broken video


A historical banknote solved through smart OSINT


Hidden Unicode characters revealing invisible flags


A flawed balance system exploitable through floating-point logic



And finally, a reminder that sometimes the real solution is simply to wait
Each problem encouraged thinking beyond the obvious, reinforcing the idea that in CTFs — just like in security — assumptions are often your biggest weakness.
This writeup walks through the mindset, tools, and techniques used to solve every challenge step by step, making it useful not only as a solution guide but also as a learning resource for beginners and intermediate players alike.

title: Breaking JWT: Common JWT Vulnerabilities
content:
SON Web Tokens (JWTs)

are a compact, URL-safe way of securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object. They are widely used in modern web applications for authentication, authorization, and session management.
A JWT consists of three parts:

header.payload.signature

Header – Algorithm and token type
Payload – Claims (user data)
Signature – Ensures integrity and authenticity


Because JWTs are stateless, servers usually don’t store session data — which makes implementation mistakes extremely dangerous.

Types of JWT Vulnerabilities & Bypass Techniques


1. Flawed JWT Signature Verification

2. Accepting Arbitrary Signatures (alg: none)
3. Brute-Forcing Weak Secret Keys (HS256)
4. JWT Revocation Bypass (Blacklist Bypass)
5. Self-Signed JWT via jwk Header Injection
6. Self-Signed JWT via jku Header Injection
7. JWT Bypass via kid Parameter Injection
8. Algorithm Confusion (RS256 → HS256)
9. Algorithm Confusion (No Exposed Key)



References & Practice Labs

https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/tree/master/JSON%20Web%20Token

title: RCSC Presents Resurrection CTF 2025 web & pwn category writeup
content:
Hi, today I’m sharing an overview writeup of the web & pwn challenges from “RCSC Presents Resurrection CTF 2025” that I authored (except Search Party). The set includes: The Hidden Shelf, Insufficient Balance, Search Party, A Session Hijinks, f1ow_&_f1ow, and Func…—each designed to test practical exploitation mindset, from simple logic abuse to classic memory corruption.

In the web category, the challenges focused on noticing what the application “tries to hide” and then proving it with clean enumeration or request tampering. The Hidden Shelf was all about identifying inconsistent product listings and using controlled brute-force on /product/ until the hidden entry revealed the flag. Insufficient Balance explored insecure server-side price handling, where the purchase logic trusted a malformed input structure—making it possible to buy the expensive flag item without paying the real cost. Search Party (not my authored one) leaned into client-side analysis: obfuscated JavaScript hinted at a secret route, leading to a hidden endpoint where the flag was encoded as character codes.

A Session Hijinks moved from JWT assumptions into real session exploitation: a Flask signed cookie contained the role, and with the secret key recovered via wordlist brute-force, the cookie could be re-signed with role: admin to unlock restricted content and obtain the flag. This challenge was meant to reinforce how dangerous weak Flask secrets are, especially when role-based authorization is stored client-side.

In the pwn category, the problems were intentionally beginner-friendly but satisfying. f1ow_&_f1ow rewarded understanding of program behavior and boundaries—where a long input triggers the “overflow detected” flow and directly reveals the flag. Finally, Func… was a classic ret2win: a vulnerable gets()-based buffer overflow with an unused win() function. By calculating the correct offset and returning to win(), the server prints the flag—simple, clean, and a perfect introduction to control-flow hijacking.

title: RUET Cyber Fest 2025 -CTF My Problems Writeup
content:
Today, I’m sharing an overview of the writeups for the challenges I created for RUET Cyber Fest 2025 CTF. These tasks were split across Web and Pwn, and each one was designed to teach (or test) a different skill—ranging from simple request tampering and input validation mistakes to classic memory corruption and logic-based exploitation. For anyone who wants to practice, I’ll also provide a Drive link containing the full challenge files in “RUET Cyber Fest 2025 CTF.zip”.

On the Web side, the challenges focused heavily on real-world bug patterns. Broken Calculator was a basic but fun one: the UI “broke” the negative key, but the backend still trusted user input—so intercepting the request and sending a negative value directly was enough to grab the reward. Tap Tap explored client-server trust issues in point systems, where modifying the request parameter allowed instant farming of points to purchase the flag. File introduced path traversal with an extra twist—direct access to flag.txt was blocked, but appending a null byte bypassed the check and exposed the internal file. Developer was centered around an IDOR-style logic flaw: a password reset flow allowed swapping the target user ID, leading to admin takeover (with the final step involving common admin username guessing). The Password was a classic SQL injection challenge; using UNION SELECT against a SQLite-backed app made it possible to enumerate tables and dump user credentials, where the admin password directly contained the flag.

The Pwn challenges were built to be approachable while still rewarding careful reading of code behavior. Insane Story wasn’t about ROP or gadgets—just logic: the program printed the flag only if the input length crossed a threshold, so sending a story longer than ~1000 bytes triggered the flag path. A Secure Fest was a clean buffer overflow via strcpy() into a small buffer; the goal was to overwrite the return address and redirect execution to a hidden secret_function() that prints the flag. Finally, Easy Maze was a speed-based web maze inspired by earlier CTFs: reaching the finish under 40 seconds is unrealistic manually due to network latency, so the intended solve was automation—find the correct path once, then replay it with a Python script using authenticated requests to beat the timer reliably.

title: First time at HackerOne Bug Hunt — and made it to the Finals.
content:
This year, I took my first step into the world of HackerOne Bug Hunt, organized by Bug Bounty Community Bangladesh (BBCBD), not knowing exactly where the journey would lead—only that I wanted to challenge myself and test my skills in a real-world, competitive cybersecurity environment. What began as curiosity and passion for ethical hacking soon turned into an intense and rewarding experience filled with learning, problem-solving, and self-discovery.

As a first-time participant, the qualifiers pushed me to think beyond theory. Each challenge required careful observation, logical exploitation, and a deep understanding of how modern web applications fail under real attack scenarios. The experience reinforced the importance of responsible disclosure, patience, and creativity—values that lie at the heart of ethical hacking.

Being selected as a Finalist (Top 55 Hackers) for HackerOne Bug Hunt 2026 is an honor I truly value, especially knowing the level of talent within Bangladesh’s cybersecurity community. Competing under my HackerOne username “Devil_32”, this achievement represents not just a result, but the countless hours spent learning, practicing, failing, and improving.

HackerOne Bug Hunt has grown into a flagship event since its inception, and being part of it for the first time has given me exposure to how real-world security challenges are approached by professionals, students, and researchers alike. The journey has strengthened my confidence, sharpened my technical mindset, and motivated me to continue pursuing ethical hacking and bug bounty research more seriously.

As I prepare for the final round on January 10, 2026, at the National Science and Technology Complex (NSTC), Dhaka, I look forward to learning even more, exchanging knowledge with fellow hackers, and pushing my limits further. Regardless of the outcome, this experience has already become a milestone in my cybersecurity journey—one that reminds me why I chose this path.

This is just the beginning. The hunt continues.

title: Attachment Day 01: My First Look Into Enterprise Cybersecurity
content:
On my first day of attachment, I was introduced to a broader perspective on cybersecurity. Instead of focusing only on vulnerabilities or exploits, the discussion centered on how organizations design secure architectures, manage risks, and protect complex infrastructures.

Under the guidance of **Shahab Al Yamin Chowdhury** — cybersecurity consultant and former **Group CISO at Link3 Technologies** and **CISO at UCB Fintech (Upay)** — I began exploring how cybersecurity is practiced at the enterprise level.

---

## Understanding Cybersecurity Beyond Hacking

In many cases, cybersecurity is associated with penetration testing, exploits, and vulnerability discovery. However, enterprise security focuses on a much broader area, including:

- Security architecture
- Risk management
- Security governance
- Infrastructure protection
- Compliance and frameworks

Organizations must design systems that remain **secure, resilient, and scalable** against modern cyber threats.

---

## Key Security Concepts Discussed

### AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting)

AAA is a security framework used to control and monitor access to systems.

- **Authentication** – Verifying the identity of a user.
- **Authorization** – Determining what actions the user is allowed to perform.
- **Accounting** – Tracking and logging user activities within the system.

---

### CIA Triad

The **CIA Triad** is a fundamental model in cybersecurity consisting of three principles:

- **Confidentiality** – Protecting information from unauthorized access.
- **Integrity** – Ensuring data remains accurate and unaltered.
- **Availability** – Making sure systems and data are accessible when needed.

---

### IT General Controls (ITGC)

ITGC are policies and procedures used to manage and secure an organization's IT environment.

They focus on four major areas:

- IT operations
- Access control
- Change management
- System development

These controls help reduce risks such as **unauthorized access, system errors, fraud, and data loss**.

---

### 5W1H Method

The **5W1H Method** is a structured questioning technique used to analyze problems and understand situations clearly.

It focuses on six questions:

- **What**
- **Who**
- **Where**
- **When**
- **Why**
- **How**

This method helps organizations investigate issues, identify root causes, and develop effective solutions.

---

### ISO/IEC 27001

**ISO/IEC 27001** is an international standard for **Information Security Management Systems (ISMS)**.

It provides a framework for organizations to:

- Manage information security risks
- Protect sensitive data
- Implement security policies and controls
- Continuously improve security practices

---

## Enterprise Security Technologies

We also explored various enterprise cybersecurity technologies used in modern organizations, such as:

- **SIEM** – Security monitoring and log analysis
- **IAM / PAM** – Identity and privilege access management
- **EDR / MDR** – Endpoint detection and response
- **SOAR** – Security automation and orchestration
- **CASB / CSPM** – Cloud security management
- **WAF / ZTNA / SASE** – Network and application protection

These technologies work together to create a **layered security architecture** across enterprise environments.

---

## Additional Learning Resources

- System Design 101
https://github.com/ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101

- CISO MindMap
https://rafeeqrehman.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/CISO_MindMap_2024.pdf

---

## Final Thoughts

My first day of attachment provided valuable insight into how cybersecurity works in real-world enterprise environments. It showed that security is not only about discovering vulnerabilities, but also about designing secure systems, managing risks, and implementing structured frameworks.

I would like to sincerely thank **Shahab Al Yamin Chowdhury** for sharing his knowledge and industry experience with us. His guidance helped us better understand how cybersecurity operates in large organizations and how different technologies and strategies work together to protect digital infrastructure.

This session set a strong foundation for the rest of my attachment journey, and I look forward to learning more about enterprise security practices in the coming days.

---

title: Attachment Day 02: Exploring Cybersecurity Frameworks and Enterprise Capability Models
tags: Security, Security Framework, Security Capability Model
content:
Exploring Cybersecurity Frameworks and Enterprise Capability Models

On the second day of my cybersecurity industrial attachment at G8ICT Limited, our learning session with Shahab Al Yamin Chowdhury, Cybersecurity Consultant and Enterprise Architect, focused on understanding the frameworks and capability models that organizations use to structure their cybersecurity programs.

While many academic discussions around cybersecurity concentrate on vulnerabilities, exploits, and technical tools, this session highlighted the strategic side of cybersecurity in enterprise environments. We explored how organizations design security programs using structured frameworks, governance models, and capability standards to manage risks, align technology with business objectives, and maintain resilient systems.

During the session, we were introduced to a variety of industry frameworks and models including RACI Matrix, Cybersecurity Domains, Business Capability Maps, LeanIX Business Capability Model, the NICE Workforce Framework, Zachman Framework, SFIA Skills Framework, C2M2, SAFe, and several global cybersecurity standards and control frameworks. These frameworks provide organizations with structured approaches to defining responsibilities, evaluating security maturity, developing workforce capabilities, and managing complex enterprise systems.

Another key takeaway from this session was understanding how cybersecurity is deeply connected with enterprise architecture, governance, risk management, and organizational processes. Instead of focusing only on technical defenses, enterprises rely on these frameworks to create a comprehensive security strategy that integrates people, processes, and technology.

This session provided valuable insight into how cybersecurity is practiced in real-world enterprise environments and helped bridge the gap between academic learning and industry practices.

A sincere thank you to Shahab Al Yamin Chowdhury vai for sharing his knowledge and providing such a comprehensive perspective on enterprise cybersecurity. Special thanks as well to Alin Boby vai for helping arrange this learning opportunity.
